Several Republican lawmakers raise questions and concerns about Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang, saying his ‘behavior does not support reinstatement’

Sign up to the Breaking News US email
Nvidia
’s shares have surged by 31% at the start of trading following the news. The
S+P 500
jumped 4.5% and is recovering nearly half of its brutal losses from last week, which was one of its worst since the 2008 financial crisis. Rallies for AI stocks had the
Nasdaq
composite up a market-leading 6.5%, while the
Dow Jones Industrial Average
rose 1,117 points.
Here’s
Trump
’s full social media post, in which he also called
Jensen Huang
“a Great Patriot and National Treasure”.
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!

items.title: US imposes new Iran-related sanctions
items.content:
US imposes new Iran-related sanctions
The US treasury department imposed new sanctions targeting individuals and entities involved in an Iranian "shadow banking" network, it said on Monday.
The list included eight Iranian citizens in addition to several trading entities based in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong.
The US treasury department described the network as "the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime".

items.content:
Exclusive: Services say supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces has made it ‘almost impossible’ to find refuges for trans people
There are only six beds specifically for trans victims of domestic abuse in the UK, a new report has found, with services saying it is “almost impossible” to find refuges for trans people since
the supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces
.
Galop, an LGBTQ+ anti-abuse charity, called on the government to create an emergency national fund for specialist trans refuges, as many were being turned away from mainstream services.

items.content:
Houthi-run government says Saudi air strikes killed civilians in Lahj
The Houthi government in Yemen said Saudi air strikes targeting buses in the governorate of Lahj had killed or wounded tens of civilians, rejecting earlier accusations by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government that the Houthis were responsible.
The statement described the Saudi strikes as a "horrific massacre" that amounts to a war crime.
Earlier reports of coalition air strikes on the area were published and later deleted by media outlets affiliated with Saudi Arabia.

items.title: ‘Scapegoating’: green groups condemn plan to axe Environment Agency and Natural England
items.content:
Ministers proposing to abolish the quangos in attempt to give politicians more control over what gets built and where
Scientists have accused the government of scapegoating nature for proposing to scrap the only environmental regulator with a legal duty to protect the natural world.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the independent regulator
Natural England
and the Environment Agency were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of quangos, or arm’s length bodies. Ministers are considering abolishing the two biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where.

items.title: Israeli contestant with 'peace' costume booed at Miss Universe 2026
items.content:
Israeli contestant with 'peace' costume booed at Miss Universe 2026
Submitted by
Hannah. Smith
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 14:12
Social media users slam 'audacity' of dress amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza and wars in the region
Miss Israel 2026 Danielle Yablonka, who describes herself as a Zionist, on stage during the national costume segment of the Miss Universe competition (Screengrab/Instagram: @missisrael)
Off
Miss
Israel
was booed on stage during the national costume portion of the
Miss Universe
pageant in Puerto Rico this weekend.
As Danielle Yablonka stepped out in a gold jewelled bodice, boots and crown, she spread her arms to reveal a cape depicting olive trees and Jaffa oranges, with the word “peace” written in English, Hebrew and Arabic running along the bottom.
After she came to a stop and posed for the judges, she was immediately met with loud boos that even the music couldn’t cover.
Turning around to reveal the back of the garment, she kept her arms held out to show the audience the warm-toned depiction of East Jerusalem, featuring the vibrant gold and blue of Al-Aqsa Mosque complex in the centre, surrounded by the Old City.
East Jerusalem is considered occupied under international law. It is also envisioned as the capital of an independent Palestinian state - not a part of Israel.
The glossy image - not a real photo - did not reflect the ongoing demolition of
Palestinian
homes in the city, and featured the word Jerusalem in English, Hebrew and Arabic.
The costume choice for the 25-year-old Miami-born model was met with fierce criticism on social media, with users pointing out the ongoing ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the
genocide
in Gaza.
Miss Universe Israel 2026 - National Costume
From her homeland to the global stage.
#MissUniverse2026
pic.twitter.com/Sm6tk4GN14
— Zoey talks (@bunsooooxx)
November 21, 2026
"Miss Israel gets rightfully booed at the Miss Universe pageant for having the audacity to wear a costume that says 'peace' while her country is the one preventing peace by committing genocide and brutally occupying Palestine,"
wrote
one user on X.
Others highlighted that the olive and
orange
motifs on the dress are defining symbols of Palestinian national identity.
One Reddit user summarised the sentiment of other commentators,
writing
: “The gall to put olive trees in that AI disaster while palestinians in the west bank are having their own systematically uprooted, destroying their livelihoods and heritage.”
This was particularly resonant after the olive harvest season this year, which saw a
sharp rise
in Palestinians being attacked by Israeli settlers, who carried out a reported 1,369 attacks in October alone.
The Israeli military also regularly
demolishes olive groves
and has uprooted thousands of olive trees across occupied Palestine.
'Colonial talking point'
Other users focused on the introduction given by the host, who described Israel as “the land where history lives, cultures meet, and even the desert blooms”, adding that the country “turned arid landscapes into thriving agricultural communities” as Yablonka walked on stage.
These phrases, often repeated by Israel and its supporters, have long been criticised by Palestinians as discourse that serves to justify occupation and erase Palestinian history, as well as misleadingly imply that the lands were neglected and empty before the arrival of Jewish settlers.
Historians have long refuted this, pointing to historical records of agricultural development and trade throughout Ottoman Palestine and beyond, including the production of the famous Jaffa orange.
the idea that the land was inhabitable and a desert wasteland before is one of the biggest zionist talking points btw.
https://t.co/QujyKXsAS8
— project hail malak ˚₊‧꒰ა ☆ ໒꒱ ‧₊˚ (@mxdeinhexvens)
November 22, 2026
One X user
wrote
: “The host in the background talking about Israel ‘making the desert bloom’ is such a colonial talking point."
Some other users pointed out similarities t0 the dress worn by Miss Palestine 2025, Nada Ayoub, which featured Al-Aqsa Mosque's Dome of the Rock and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, designed by Palestinian artist Neven Elkady.
They even stole Miss Palestine’s theme from last year hahahah
https://t.co/XglFXYhAS0
pic.twitter.com/OBQ7jmDKaN
— zز 🍒🇵🇸 (@z_00pIz)
November 22, 2026
Ayoub herself acknowledged the similarities in a
video
shared to Instagram following the backlash.
"I turned. The world saw Jerusalem. A year later, Miss Israel turned. Look familiar?" she wrote.
"On a stage where Jerusalem is shown, it had me questioning: Where is the Palestinian voice?" she added, touching on the irony of Miss Israel's choice to feature the Dome of the Rock given the
increasing Israeli attacks
on Al-Aqsa Mosque.
The absence of a Palestinian voice from this year's line-up was marked, and many fans took to social media to ask Ayoub why.
In 2025, Ayoub became the first Palestinian woman to represent the country in the global pageant competition, placing in the top 30. However, this year, plans to include a Miss Palestine fell through before the deadline.
Ayoub explained in her video that vast resources are needed to help a beauty queen reach the international stage, after qualifying through local and national competitions, which don’t have the structural or financial backing in Palestine.
This is compounded by the backdrop of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, making it difficult to create spaces for new talent to emerge and grow.
Ayoub appealed to Palestinian businessmen and women, organisations and institutions to back the project for the next Miss Palestine, emphasising the importance of representation of Palestinian voices in international competitions.
She added that she has largely been financing the project herself, which is why it has been difficult to realise her ambition to select a new Miss Palestine.

items.title: Talk of scrapping Natural England smacks of a government not joining the dots
items.content:
Environmentalists say abolishing independent body will make it easier for landowners and developers ‘to trash nature’
Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.
Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.

items.title: Cop31 collapses: why did climate talks fall apart? - The Latest
items.content:
Countries at the Cop31 climate summit failed to reach a keystone agreement for the first time in 17 years. The talks, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were intended to produce a pact that would have injected urgency into climate action and financing for vulnerable states. Instead, the deal failed after a standoff over fossil fuels and support for countries exposed to the climate crisis. Guardian Australia’s climate and environment reporter Graham Readfearn tells Lucy Hough why there are calls for urgent reform of the Cop process

items.content:
القوات المسلحة اليمنية

شن الطيران الحربي السعودي خلال الـ24 ساعة الماضية 67 غارةً جويةً وصاروخاً استهدف بها الأعيان المدنية في العاصمة صنعاء ومحافظات لحج وتعز والحديدة وصعدة وحجة وذلك من خلال طائرات "F-15" أقلعت من قاعدة خميس مشيط والعدوان الصاروخي من نجران، وخلفت عشرات الشهداء والجرحى من المدنيين.
ليبلغ إجمالي غارات العدوان السعودي منذ بدء التصعيد على بلدِنا 5648 غارة جوية وصاروخا.
إن الجرائم الوحشية التي ارتكبها العدو السعودي في الحديدة ولحج لن تمر مرور الكرام وستكون عواقبها عليه وخيمة بإذن الله.

Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
In late October 2024, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a military headquarters in the occupied Donetsk region, told his wife, Natalya, over the phone: “It’s horrific, what’s going on here. I’ll tell you when I get back.”
He never made it home. Five weeks later, shortly after turning 29, Bolgov walked about 300 metres from his unit’s command post near the village of Stepove into woodland and shot himself, according to a written account by his commander seen by the Guardian.

items.title: Turkish pro-Kurdish party confirms improved conditions for militant who launched peace push
items.content:
ISTANBUL, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Turkey's pro-Kurdish DEM Party called on Monday for jailed militant leader Abdullah Ocalan to be given more freedom to advance peace talks with the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party, or PKK, following an improvement in his prison conditions.
Ocalanlaunched the process in February 2025 when he called on the PKK, which he founded and led, to disband and end a decades-old conflict in which more than 40,000 people have been killed.
The PKK is designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

items.title: India's Rafale fighter jet count reduced by three after 2025 aerial battles with Pakistan
items.content:
India's Rafale fighter jet count reduced by three after 2025 aerial battles with Pakistan
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 13:01
Listing by World Air Forces increases scrutiny of India's denial of losses in conflict with Pakistan in 2025
A pilot climbs into a Rafale fighter jet before a French-Indian military exercise at Mont-de-Marsan air base, southwestern France, 26 November 2025 (Christophe Archambault/AFP).
Off
The number of active Rafale fighter jets in the Indian Air Force has
fallen
to 32 from 35 in the latest edition of an international military aviation directory, which has stirred renewed scrutiny of India's May 2025 military confrontation with Pakistan.
The revised figures, which appear in the 2027 World Air Forces directory published by British aviation magazine FlightGlobal, have renewed questions about the extent of Indian losses during Operation Sindoor.
Following the 22 April 2025 Pahalgam attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, India
launched
the military campaign on 7 May and attacked several targets deep inside Pakistan.
In the
largest jet engagements
of the 21st century, over 114 fighter jets were mobilised and engaged across the border.
Some 72 Indian Air Force (IAF) aircraft and 42 Pakistan Air Force (PAF) aircraft engaged each other in a confrontation that lasted roughly 50 minutes,
according
to military briefings and defence analyses.
Pakistan
claimed
to have shot down six Indian military aircraft, including three Rafales, during the confrontation.
New Delhi disputed the scale of Islamabad's claims but did not publish a detailed account of its own aircraft losses.
During a military briefing on 11 May, Air Marshal Awadhesh Kumar Bharti acknowledged that India had suffered aircraft losses but declined to identify the number or types involved.
“We are in a combat scenario and losses are a part of combat,” Bharti said.
India's Rahul Gandhi backs continued arms trade with Israel despite Gaza genocide
Read More »
Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan also
accepted
that India had lost aircraft during the fighting.
Asked about the losses, Chauhan said the important issue was understanding why they had occurred and how the military had responded.
India purchased 36 Rafale fighter aircraft from France under a 2016 agreement. FlightGlobal's previous edition, published in late 2025, listed 35 as active.
The latest directory has reduced that figure by three, without identifying the aircraft excluded from the active inventory or explaining the reasons for the revision.
The debate over the active fleet comes as India pursues a major expansion of its Rafale inventory.
In April 2025, India and France signed an intergovernmental agreement for the procurement of 26 Dassault Rafale Marine aircraft for the Indian Navy.
The aircraft are intended to operate from India's aircraft carriers, strengthening the Navy's carrier-based combat capabilities.
India is also
pursuing
the acquisition of 114 additional Rafale fighters for the Air Force. The proposed acquisition is estimated to cost about 3.25 trillion rupees ($39bn), according to reports.
The proposed purchase would be one of India's largest fighter aircraft acquisitions and comes amid concerns about the declining strength of its combat aircraft fleet.

items.title: Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
items.content:
Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 14:00
Israeli law professor Eliav Lieblich says language used by Myanmar officials mild compared to Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and others
Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks on during a speech at the Israeli Knesset during the opening day of the new parliament in Jerusalem on 10 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
Israel
will probably lose the
genocide case brought by South Africa
if the
International Court of Justice
(ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to
find Myanmar responsible for genocide
against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.
“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.
“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he
wrote
in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”
The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against
Palestinians
in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.
To prove the genocide, the ICJ first had to prove that genocidal acts were committed, then that there was a “specific intent” by the Myanmar state to destroy the group.
Genocidal intent
Genocidal intent is rarely ever stated explicitly, so courts usually rely on circumstantial evidence. And where there are various possible intentions, such as military objectives, the court then establishes whether genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the conduct.
Myanmar argued that its campaign against the Rohingya was a counter-insurgency operation and that other motives that could explain its conduct included a desire to drive the Rohingya out or to punish the civilian population.
But the court rejected all these explanations and said the “only reasonable inference” to be drawn from Myanmar’s conduct was genocide.
Lieblich argued that Israeli officials themselves have provided evidence of genocidal intent that is easier to prove than that in the Myanmar case.
'Given the statements by senior officials, the overall context and other aspects of the case, I think Israel would still most likely lose under the majority’s approach'
- Eliav Lieblich, Tel Aviv University
“The statements by senior Myanmar officials about the Rohingya that the court relied on seem mild compared with what has come out of the Netanyahu–Ben Gvir–Smotrich gang,” he said. “Add the rampage in the West Bank, and in my view Israel is in a very bad position.”
The nine judges in the majority found that the scale and pattern of the violence made an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya the only reasonable inference.
The six dissenters accepted that Myanmar’s forces committed grave atrocities but took a narrower view of their proven scale and reach. They considered forced displacement a reasonable alternative explanation, which meant the test for proving genocidal intent was not met.
Lieblich said two parts of the majority’s interpretation of the Genocide Convention, taken together, “fundamentally undermine Israel’s position”.
The first concerns forced displacement. The court found that expelling people in harsh conditions and preventing them from returning home can cause the kind of serious mental harm covered by Article II(b) of the convention. The second concerns what it means to destroy a group.
In Lieblich’s reading, the required intent can include an aim to prevent the group from continuing to function as a group.
Lieblich said the implications for Gaza become clearer when Israel’s displacement of Palestinians and destruction of neighbourhoods are considered alongside conditions in the areas people fled to and statements by senior Israeli officials.
ICJ ruling on Rohingya genocide could strengthen South Africa's case against Israel
Read More »
He referred to “a defining moment” when Avraham Zarbiv, a military reservist who operated a bulldozer in Gaza and publicly celebrated the demolitions, lit a torch at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony.
Lieblich said Israel could argue that Hamas’s military capabilities and the nature of the fighting in Gaza set the case apart from Myanmar’s campaign against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.
Israel could also point to the scale of the 7 October attacks and argue that its actions were aimed at putting pressure on Hamas and destroying it.
“Given the statements by senior officials, the overall context and other aspects of the case, I think Israel would still most likely lose under the majority’s approach,” he said.
For Lieblich, the split between the judges reflected differences over how to assess the evidence, what constitutes genocide and how sharply the law should distinguish it from other grave crimes.
“Either way, anyone who, like Myanmar, has to defend themselves against accusations of genocide by arguing that their actions amounted to other serious crimes has already lost,” he wrote.
Lieblich said he was surprised to learn that Myanmar had set up a commission of inquiry that found serious crimes had been committed during the military operation. In his view, the inquiry did little to help Myanmar’s case because it did not adequately investigate the genocide allegation before the court.
“In Israel, even the opposition has yet to propose a commission of inquiry to examine these aspects,” he wrote.
'Substantial' part
The court held that Myanmar committed genocide against 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, a region in western Myanmar along the border with Bangladesh. The figure amounts to roughly 58 percent of the 1.4 million Rohingya that Myanmar said lived in the country at the time.
The group targeted was large enough to constitute a “substantial part” of the Rohingya population under the Genocide Convention.
The court found three acts of genocide committed against men, women and children: the killing of 10,000 Rohingya, causing serious physical or psychological harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births.
The court confirmed what international law has previously held, that a state does not have to do everything it can to destroy the group, or to kill all its members, in order to be held responsible for genocide.
The ICJ also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces, failed to punish genocide and other acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention, and failed to enact legislation giving effect to the treaty.
It also ruled that Myanmar breached one of the court’s four provisional measures, a 2020 order to preserve evidence, by building a government base on former Rohingya village sites and destroying the remains of at least five other villages.

"This has led to the complete destruction of these facilities (and) the disruption of telecommunications and internet services," they said.

items.title: Israeli army suicides reach highest level since 2010: Press review
items.content:
Israeli army suicides reach highest level since 2010: Press review
Submitted by
Nadav Rapaport
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 14:10
Meanwhile, an army officer warns ‘Jewish terrorism’ in the West Bank could spread into Israel, and Kan 11 is urged to censor Gaza human shields investigation
An Israeli army soldier looks at destroyed buildings in the Gaza Strip as troops stand on the boundary with the Palestinian territory, on 13 August 2025 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off
Israeli military suicides reach 16-year high
A total of 23 serving
Israeli
military personnel have died by suicide since the beginning of this year, the highest number recorded in the army since 2010, Haaretz
reported
on Monday.
At least 17 former soldiers also died by suicide in the past year, shortly after being discharged from military service, bringing the total number of serving and former soldiers who took their own lives to 40.
Suicides are not confined to Israel's military. Haaretz noted that five police officers also died by suicide in 2026.
According to official Israeli military data cited by the report, 73 officers and soldiers have died by suicide since the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on 7 October.
However, the actual number of war-related suicides is likely to be much higher, as the military's figures include only personnel who died while still serving.
"This war is an unprecedented event in terms of the level of distress and burnout of the soldiers who took part in it," a mental health academic at the University of Haifa told Haaretz.
"The coming years are critical, perhaps even dramatic, with regard to suicide rates."
Israeli officer warns of ‘Jewish terrorism’
An Israeli senior military officer has warned that attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are organised and involve thousands of people, Israel's Channel 12 News
reported
on Monday.
"These are organised terrorist organisations. They have an agenda of expelling Arabs and are working to achieve it," the officer said, referring to settler militias known as the Hilltop Youth.
'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
Read More »
"This is Jewish terrorism, and what is disturbing is the scale," he added. "It's already a few thousand individuals, not hundreds. It's not a handful. It's already a large population that does not obey the law."
The officer warned that "everything that happens there will spread into the centre of Israel", saying attacks against Palestinians inside Israel were inevitable unless the state changed its approach towards the militias.
The senior officer's comments contradict those of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has repeatedly played down attacks by the Hilltop Youth,
describing the perpetrators
as a "handful of juvenile delinquents".
On Saturday, armed settler militias
attacked
several Palestinian villages near Ramallah, setting vehicles alight and spray-painting racist slogans on homes.
According to Channel 12 News, officials within Israel's security establishment said amid the attacks that the state was not doing enough to prevent settler violence against Palestinians.
Kan 11 urged to censor Gaza human shields investigation
A  right-wing Israeli NGO has called on the country's public broadcaster, Kan 11, to censor an investigation into the Israeli army's use of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip as human shields, Channel 14 News
reported
on Monday.
According to the report, B'tsalmo, an organisation that monitors journalists and academics critical of Israel, sent a letter to Kan 11 chief executive Golan Yochpaz urging him not to air the investigation, which is scheduled for Wednesday.
'Foreign entities could use the materials that will be broadcast to advance investigations and requests for arrest warrants against Israeli soldiers'
- Channel 14
A promotional clip
posted on X
last week said the investigation would examine how Israeli soldiers used Palestinians as human shields during the genocide in Gaza, in a practice known as the "Mosquito Protocol".
"Foreign entities could use the materials that will be broadcast to advance investigations and requests for arrest warrants against Israeli soldiers and commanders," Channel 14 reported, adding that B'tsalmo had asked Yochpaz to submit the investigation to the Israeli army for review.
On Sunday, Israeli journalist Hanoch Daum
attacked
the investigation in a Facebook post, defending the military's use of the so-called Mosquito Protocol.
"Between the lives of this team of fighters I met and the Gazans, I know whom I choose," Daum wrote, adding a message he said he had received from an Israeli soldier shortly after publishing his post.
"I remember at least 3-4 cases where a mosquito saved our lives and even exploded in front of us," the alleged soldier wrote, referring to Palestinians forced by the army to walk ahead of advancing Israeli forces in Gaza to draw fire from Hamas.
The soldier also expressed hope that the Israeli public "will understand the difference that after 7 October, we come before everyone".
The message asserted that Israeli lives should take priority over Palestinian lives.

items.title: Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
items.content:
Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sat, 11/21/2026 - 18:15
The Latin American country pitched the idea to diplomats in The Hague despite rights advocates warning against attempts to curb the court's mission
Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio listen during a news briefing in the White House on 20 November 2026 (AFP)
Off
Guatemala has circulated a proposal to member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) that closely echoed demands made by the
United States
and
Israel
to severely restrict the court's powers, Middle East Eye can reveal.
The three-page paper was submitted at a closed-door retreat for ambassadors from ICC member states in The Hague on 18 November, less than two weeks before the court's Assembly of States Parties (ASP) opens its annual session.
The proposal advocated for dialogue with the US over curbing the ICC's ability to pursue cases involving nationals of countries that aren't members of the court, such as the US, Israel and Russia.
MEE understands that Washington's G7 allies, including the UK, Germany and Italy, expressed a readiness to discuss similar proposals with the US but were reluctant to advocate the idea publicly.
As a result, Guatemala, a Latin American country allied with Israel and the US, decided to take the lead and draft the proposal.
The document, seen by MEE, reflects Washington's longstanding opposition to the prosecution of Israeli leaders and the court's ability to also prosecute US officials for crimes committed on the territory of member states.
The paper floats requiring consent from a suspect's country of nationality even when the alleged crimes took place on the territory of an ICC member state.
Dapo Akande elected as ICJ judge, restoring British presence inside highest UN court
Read More »
It also calls for an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on immunity and advances arguments that echo Israel's challenge to the way the ICC prosecutor handled the Palestine investigation.
The proposal also says Washington's views should be taken into account in discussions about the court's governance because the US hosts assembly sessions in New York.
This year's session, which begins 30 November, was moved to The Hague amid concerns that US sanctions and visa restrictions could limit participation.
The assembly president and secretariat are expected to draft a resolution regarding Guatemala’s proposal and to circulate it to member states for negotiation, sources told MEE.
MEE reached out to Guatemala, the UK, Canada, Italy, Germany, Japan, France and the ASP for comment.
MEE understands that France appeared to be the only country in the group willing to consider talks aimed at protecting the court from efforts to weaken its jurisdiction.
The UK foreign office declined to comment on discussions between state parties prior to the ASP. A source reiterated that the UK supports "constructive and inclusive dialogue" with non-member states.
Preconditions for lifting sanctions
The initiative came after Washington imposed far-reaching sanctions on the court in October while granting the court a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands.
Once fully in effect in April, the sanctions could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations.
Earlier sanctions had already targeted half the court's judges, and all top prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025 to penalise the officials for their work on the Palestine and Afghanistan investigations.
The idea of dialogue with the US was a key topic in last year's Assembly of States Parties in December after an EU diplomat presented the US demands for discussion. The US made those demands as a condition for lifting sanctions.
MEE revealed at the time that member states disagreed on what a dialogue would entail, and by the end of the conference agreed that any talks should aim at ensuring the independence and effectiveness of the court.
'The one thing that cannot be part of a dialogue in the face of a treaty negotiation is the jurisdictional provisions of the Rome Statute'
- Kimberly Prost, Canadian ICC judge
The Guatemalan proposal is consistent with
MEE's previous reporting
on US demands, including the fact that Washington had pressed the court to drop its investigations into Palestine and Afghanistan and urged member states to amend the Rome Statute to bar prosecutions of nationals of countries outside the court.
The US and Israel, non-members of the ICC, have both rejected the court's jurisdiction over their nationals.
Territorial jurisdiction is a foundational principle of the ICC since its establishment in 2002.
The Rome Statute, its founding treaty, allows the ICC to prosecute genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed on the territory of a member state, regardless of the suspect’s nationality.
That provision allowed the court to investigate alleged crimes by US personnel in Afghanistan and provided the basis for arrest warrants issued in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes in Gaza.
Palestine has been a member of the court since 2015.
In a controversial decision earlier this month, ICC judges
ordered the closure
of the court's Afghanistan investigation that covered alleged war crimes by US forces, despite ongoing attempts by prosecutors to appeal the decision.
Instead, they lauched a new inquiry focused solely on alleged crimes by the Taliban, the de facto Afghan government.
The move raised questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies.
Consent and immunity
Trump's executive order has allowed the US to sanction those who help the ICC investigate or prosecute certain individuals without their home country’s consent.
In an apparent alignment with the US, the Guatemalan paper recommends making consent from a suspect's country an additional requirement even where the court already has jurisdiction on territorial grounds.
It also proposes asking the ICJ, the UN's highest court, for an advisory opinion on Article 98, a controversial provision in the Statute which addresses whether immunity can prevent a country from handing a foreign official over to the ICC.
ICC judges order end to investigation into alleged crimes by US forces in Afghanistan
Read More »
The paper also echoes Israel's
unsuccessful bid
to have the ICC give it another chance to investigate its own crimes in Gaza domestically.
Under the court's rules, known as "complimentarity," countries have the first chance to investigate and prosecute alleged crimes. The ICC can step in if the accused country is unwilling or unable to do so genuinely.
The ICC opened its investigation into alleged crimes in Palestine in March 2021 and formally notified Israel that year.
Israel later argued that the events of 7 October 2023 and a new request by seven member states to launch additional investigations had changed the scope of the investigation and that prosecutors should have notified it again.
This notice explains what the investigation will cover and gives the concerned state a chance to argue that it is already investigating the same matters itself, a principle designed to stop duplication.
Judges rejected Israel's arguments in November 2024, and appeals judges upheld that decision in December 2025.
The appeals judges, however, are still examining Israel's separate
challenge
to the court's jurisdiction in the Palestine situation.
'Clear red lines'
Kimberly Prost, a Canadian ICC judge who was part of Canada's delegation at the 1998 conference that negotiated the Rome Statute, told MEE that territorial jurisdiction was "at the heart of the Rome Statute".
"You can have a dialogue with the US. I believe in diplomacy. I believe in discussions," she said during a briefing with journalists on Thursday at the ICC.
But Prost said she had told diplomats there had to be "clear red lines" in talks with Washington and called for "strong measures" alongside statements and diplomacy.
Prost was not commenting on any particular proposal. She was responding to a question by MEE regarding a Dutch report claiming the Netherlands was involved in dialogue with the US over the demands. The
Dutch
foreign ministry has dismissed the report as inaccurate.
Prost was a member of the 2020 appeals chamber that authorised the
Afghanistan investigation
, which could cover alleged crimes by US personnel. She was sanctioned by the US last summer over that role.
She is one of three ICC judges who have sued the Trump administration over the
sanctions
.
Kimberly Prost, ICC judge, speaks to journalists at the court's headquarters in The Hague on 19 November 2026 (MEE/Sondos Asem)
"There may be things that could be done under the rules. Maybe we need some clarification on legal points that could go to the ICJ or wherever. But the one thing that cannot be part of a dialogue in the face of a treaty negotiation is the jurisdictional provisions of the Rome Statute," she said.
"You can't just change that because a group of states decide that it's inconvenient at this point in time," she added.
'Death knell'
Meanwhile, Agnes Callamard, the secretary general of Amnesty International,
publicly denounced the US demands
, but said she was not privy to the Guatemala proposal.
She said Canada, Britain, Italy, Germany and Japan were "looking for ways of appeasing the US, which means negotiating with them over their demands".
"The American demands are a death knell for the independence of the International Criminal Court," she told MEE.
"There is no room for negotiation. The only option is to protect the integrity and the independence of the ICC."
Callamard said Amnesty had raised its concerns with the governments involved.
"Those governments stand publicly for international justice and the rule of law," she said, citing the leaders of Britain and Canada. "Well, now they need to act according to their words."

items.content:
المتحدث الرسمي للقوات المسلحة اليمنية العميد يحيى سريع: في تمام الساعة 11:36صباحاً توجه تشكيل حربي سعودي من نوع "F-15" إلى محافظة تعز ولحج بعد إقلاعه من قاعدة خميس مشيط، وعند الساعة 12:40م نفذ عملية استهداف لعدد من الباصات ووسائل نقل بضائع عامة في منطقة معبق بمديرية المقاطرة وذلك بثماني غارات جوية بقنابل أمريكية نوع "GBU-49" و "GBU-12" مرتكبا جريمة وحشية ومخلفاً عشرات الشهداء والجرحى من المدنيين وغادر منطقة الاستهداف عند الساعة 12:55م وعاد إلى نفس القاعدة.
إن هذه الجريمة الوحشية لن تمر دون رد وعقاب بإذن الله.

items.title: Meet the Pacific Islanders standing for Palestine against Christian Zionism
items.content:
Meet the Pacific Islanders standing for Palestine against Christian Zionism
Submitted by
Tarek Yousef Tahan
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 11:00
In Fiji, Samoa and other islands, deep-rooted evangelical Zionism is being challenged
Mara Mahoney, Michel Mulipola and James Bhagwan are all standing in solidarity with Palestinians across the Pacific Islands (Supplied/MEE)
Off
Michel Mulipola is a comic book artist and former professional wrestler. He’s also an activist for indigenous self-determination in
Palestine
and across the Pacific Islands, as well as a former Green Party candidate in New Zealand.
It’s in keeping with his family history. Mulipola’s great-grandfather, Mataʻutia Karauna Solomona, was a Samoan resistance leader and secretary of the Mau movement, which sought to free Western Samoa of colonial rule in the 1920s and 1930s.
Solomona’s arrest resulted in a massacre of unarmed protesters by the New Zealand military and police.
“So, I guess activism or even just fighting for freedom, for sovereignty, is in my blood,” says Mulipola, who has received media attention for his customised image of the Palestinian flag using traditional Samoan petroglyphs.
The artwork, which incorporates symbols drawn from Samoan cultural traditions, became a way for Mulipola to explain why he believed his people should stand with Palestinians.
Samoans around the world grew more curious, and have carried the flag at Palestine demonstrations. But the response was not all positive.
“Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific,” Mulipola tells Middle East Eye in a video call interview.
A self-described atheist, Mulipola was accused of not being truly Samoan, just because he did not support Israel.
'Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific'
-
Michel Mulipola, comic book artist and activist
These reactions exposed a deeper tension present in the Pacific islands since even before the start of
Israel’s genocide in Gaza
.
A small but growing number of mainly young Pasifika intellectuals, theologians, and activists are pushing back against decades of deep missionary and elder evangelical conditioning.
This conditioning, heavily influenced by Christian Zionists from the
United States
, saw support for
Israel
become intertwined with local cultural identity, so that questioning someone’s political beliefs came to feel like questioning one’s own people.
Across the Pacific, a region with diverse Indigenous cultures, histories and Christian traditions, activists and church leaders' arguments are not simply about Palestine.
They are also about how communities understand colonialism, Indigenous identity, religious authority and the right of peoples to determine their own futures.
Colonial Christianity
The Pacific's relationship with Christianity is complex. Missionaries arrived in many islands from the late 18th century onwards, and the religion became deeply embedded in the social and cultural life of many communities.
But the growth of Christian Zionism in the region is something different.
According to Reverend James Bhagwan, general secretary of the Pacific Conference of Churches (PCC), which represents churches of mixed Indo-Fijian and other heritages, the more recent growth of Christian Zionism has taken place alongside the expansion of newer evangelical and Pentecostal movements.
Reverend James Bhagwan says 'Christian Zionism is not a new thing' in the Pacific Islands (Supplied)
“Christian Zionism is not a new thing. It has been slowly creeping into different spaces over the last 40 years,” he says.
Bhagwan’s ecumenical organisation brings together 35 national denominations and 11 national councils of churches across 20 Pacific Island states and territories.
Its work includes advocating for Indigenous self-determination in places such as West Papua, New Caledonia (Kanaky) and French Polynesia.
For Bhagwan, that work creates a moral obligation to engage with Palestine, too.
“We cannot pick and choose what self-determination we support,” he said. The Methodist minister believes that some Pacific Christians have difficulty distinguishing between the Israel described in biblical texts, the modern state of Israel, Judaism and Zionism.
In his view, this can lead to political positions being formed through religious identification rather than a fuller understanding of the realities facing Palestinians.
Along with Bhagwan, Mulipola points to a lack of awareness about Palestinian Christians.
He told a story about Brian Tamaki, the leader of Destiny Church, a conservative Pentecostal movement founded in New Zealand. Tamaki has led pro-Israel rallies in New Zealand.
“I remember they were counter-protesting a Palestine action, and he was spouting off his hateful Christian rhetoric,” Mulipola recalls. “My good friend Rand Hazel jumped on the megaphone and said: ‘I’m a Palestinian Christian, born in Jerusalem, my people spoke Aramaic, the language of Jesus…’ and Tamaki was gobsmacked.”
Some communities, he says, have been taken in by Eurocentric propaganda portraying all Palestinians as Muslims and demanding unconditional support for the gathering of all Jews in the holy land.
Growing up on myths
In Fiji, journalist and activist Mara Mahoney says the connection between religious belief and national identity can be particularly difficult to challenge.
Mahoney grew up in the village of Savusavu on evangelical Christian Bible study, church attendance and Christian schooling, which shaped her understanding of the world from an early age.
'When you're trying to speak facts with people… you're trying to talk about the Nakba… people will just be like, well, who are we to question God?'
-
Mara Mahoney, Fijian writer
She recalls being taught that Israel was home to God's chosen people, and that some Fijians descended from the lost tribes of Israel, a belief that could make questioning support for the modern Israeli state feel like questioning one’s own faith.
Mahoney’s own political awakening came when she left her hometown to study at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. It was there that she learned about colonialism and Indigenous struggles in the Pacific, including those in Hawaii, West Papua and New Caledonia (Kanaky).
She says missionaries had used Fijian oral storytelling and pseudo-genealogical traditions to construct narratives connecting Fijian origins to Israel. These stories, Mahoney argues, were subsequently presented to communities as accounts of their own ancestry.
The historical question is significant, but it requires careful treatment. Research by anthropologist Lynda Newland
documents
how missionary ideas about Fijian origins and the lost tribes of Israel developed between 1835 and Fiji's cession to
Britain
in 1874.
Newland's research establishes that these ideas have a historical basis in missionary discourse and that they became influential among some Indigenous Fijian clans and church groups.
Mara Mahoney is a writer and activist from Fiji (Supplied)
For Mahoney, these narratives help explain why some Fijians find it harder to question political positions associated with that connection.
“When you're trying to speak facts with people… you're trying to talk about the Nakba… people will just be like, well, who are we to question God?” she says.
The issue is not simply that people hold a religious belief, Mahoney argues. It is that questioning the belief can mean confronting an entire system of education, family expectations and identity.
The cost of challenging the narrative
“The Christianity that was kind of brought to our shores was built on fear,” Mulipola says.
“You hear people calling themselves God-fearing people, and I'm like, I've never liked that term because ruling through fear is dangerous.
“It's manipulative. It's not a loving relationship. It's an abusive one. And so many people fear the repercussions of speaking up or speaking against it.”
Mulipola describes the Samoan concept of fa'aaloalo, often associated with respect and deference, as one factor shaping how people respond to authority and adhere to Christian Zionism.
Michel Mulipola pictured at a Palestine demonstration (Supplied)
In his interpretation, the expectation to respect elders and authority figures can reinforce a reluctance to question religious leaders or teachings. Mahoney says a similar dynamic exists in Fiji.
Mulipola believes this dynamic has been compounded by forms of Christianity introduced through colonial rule, in which obedience and unquestioning faith can become closely linked.
Pasifika-Palestinian solidarity
The connection between the former wrestler's family history and the Palestinian struggle is not merely symbolic. He sees both as struggles over sovereignty, dignity and the right of a people to determine their future.
'You hear people calling themselves God-fearing people, and I'm like, I've never liked that term because ruling through fear is dangerous'
-
Michel Mulipola
Pacific concerns for family and community, he argues, are not incompatible with supporting Palestinians.
Mulipola’s artwork attempts to make that connection visible: using Samoan symbols to tell a Palestinian story and inviting viewers to recognise the similarities between different histories of dispossession and resistance.
Mahoney uses social media, particularly TikTok, to share information and encourage discussion. She’s trying to build it into traditional practice.
“There's this concept in a lot of Pacific islands called talanoa, which is just meaningful dialogue - it’s not an interrogation trying to prove I'm right… it's just sitting down and being curious about what the other person has to say,” she says.
At times, Mahoney acknowledges, she has struggled to maintain this, especially with family members who hold opposing views.
Mulipola, agrees, saying, “the wrong approach would be... aggressiveness, as much as they irritate and piss me off… it's about the energy you put out there... You've got to meet them with the facts and a measured response, but in ways that resonate.”
He refers to an encounter where he shocked a fellow Samoan by showing a Gaza Health Ministry report documenting entire families being wiped off the register.
‘Appalling’: Samoa to open Israel embassy in Jerusalem, sparking criticism
Read More »
Just as in many Middle Eastern and Palestinian cultures, tight-knit and large extended family networks are sacred to Pacific Islanders.
“Tell me more about that,” is the kind of response Mahoney admires in friends who can engage with relatives who have strongly pro-Israel views.
Mahoney says that, when people are given room to speak, some privately acknowledge that the killing of civilians is wrong, even if they don’t challenge the wider ideology.
She also acknowledges that many people in Fiji, which alongside Papua New Guinea and Nauru opened embassies in Jerusalem, have never met a Palestinian and have limited awareness of the existence of Palestinian Christians.
Bhagwan similarly believes that stronger engagement between Palestinian Christians and Pacific churches could help broaden the discussion, and suggests building relationships between people working on self-determination in Palestine and across the Pacific, particularly by involving younger generations.
Mulipola, meanwhile, sees art as one way of creating such human connections and shared cultural concepts: the Samoan word mau, associated with steadfastness and resistance, and the Palestinian concept of sumud, or steadfastness.
From solidarity to political change
The Pacific's diplomatic positions on Palestine are varied, and voting records at the United Nations show that most governments in the region either vote against, abstain or are absent during UN votes concerning Palestine.
In mid-November,
votes
on Palestinian self-determination, refugee aid, and illegal settlements were more varied.
Several traditional allies of Israel - including the Marshall Islands, Samoa, and Tuvalu - quietly softened their stance from outright opposition to abstentions or absences, even as Micronesia, Palau, and Nauru held firm alongside Israel, while Fiji, Tonga, and Papua New Guinea split their votes across the resolutions.
Palestine solidarity has been cracked down on,
especially in Fiji
.
“Those who organise gatherings and demonstrations, it's all illegal; they're not allowed,” Mahoney says. “Whenever they try to apply for march permits, they're denied. Whenever they try to do demonstrations, they are met with warnings from police…”
‘Britain can stop this’: The East Jerusalem yeshiva taking UK charity money and planning expansion
Read More »
Bhagwan argues that international diplomacy is often shaped by pragmatism, not just religious dogma: Pacific governments face urgent development and climate challenges and seek partnerships, investment and assistance, where Israel and the US, he says, have the upper hand.
“I think when it comes to the global space and the multilateral systems and international politics, the reality is that it's deeply pragmatic,” the minister says.
“And that places Palestine in a vulnerable space because Israel has more to offer than you do, right? And that's what it comes down to. We are a region, for example, that is affected by climate change and every other kind of development issue."
“Israel knows this," Mulipola says, "so they'd be making huge plays in the Pacific by offering monetary support and being part of the Pacific Leaders Forum next year… They have utilised Christian Zionism and the Christian ties to push their case.”
Palestine, in contrast, “doesn’t have the resources, doesn’t have the political power to be in those spaces”, says Mulipola.
He believes political change has historically come from the bottom up, and Mahoney, too, sees hope in younger Fijians who are increasingly willing to question beliefs they once accepted uncritically.
They acknowledge, though, the change in attitudes won't happen overnight, and some minds are too rigid to change.
“There are lots of people who have closed minds and closed hearts and don't want to hear anything else because the fear inside them is so strong,” Mulipola says.
“But for the ones who you know are listening actively, there's hope.”

items.title: Israel kills Palestinians in Gaza as aid blockade and winter floods deepen suffering
items.content:
Israel kills Palestinians in Gaza as aid blockade and winter floods deepen suffering
Submitted by
Elis Gjevori
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 11:26
Unrwa worker killed in Jabalia as Israeli attacks continue across the Gaza Strip
Displaced Palestinian children participate in a "Will and Life" race in Jabalia, northern Gaza Strip, on 22 November 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP)
Off
Israel
killed an aid worker for the UN agency for
Palestinian
refugees, Unrwa, early on Monday morning in the Jabalia refugee camp in the northern Gaza Strip, local Palestinian media
reported
.
If confirmed by Unrwa, it would add to the more than 395 personnel and affiliated workers for the UN aid body killed by Israel in Gaza since October 2023.
Several other Palestinians were wounded across the strip, including one seriously, after an Israeli drone shelled a group of people near the Al-Tawba Mosque in Jabalia.
Israeli attacks also killed at least four Palestinians and wounded more than 33 others over the weekend, the Palestinian health ministry reported on Monday.
Israel has violated the ceasefire agreement, which took effect on 11 October 2025, every day since then, killing at least 1,675 Palestinians and wounding more than 6,095 others.
It also continues to restrict the flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza.
On Sunday, the Palestinian Press Agency reported that Israel had allowed 191 aid trucks into the enclave, far fewer than the 600 trucks per day agreed under the ceasefire.
'Throw the keys back to the UN': Trump-appointed Board of Peace adviser says Israel blocking efforts
Read More »
An Al Jazeera Arabic satellite analysis published on Sunday showed persistent queues of aid trucks on the
Egyptian
side of the Rafah crossing. Its open-source unit measured a line approximately 1.1km long on 17 November, while satellite images from 10 and 12 November showed similar congestion.
The United Nations World Food Programme warned last week that conditions for Palestinians in Gaza remain bleak.
More than 1.7 million Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, many more than a dozen times, while 1.98 million need shelter assistance out of Gaza's pre-war population of 2.3 million.
More than 50 percent of Gaza's 1,700 displacement sites are in flood-prone areas, leaving Palestinians exposed to flooding during the winter months. Floods have damaged 40,000 shelters in November alone.
Al Jazeera Arabic reported that a mother living in a tent used the burial shroud of her son, who was killed by Israel, to plug holes in the shelter.
Since the start of the Gaza genocide in October 2023, Israel has killed at least 74,742 Palestinians and wounded more than 176,227 others. The death toll is widely believed to be much higher, with bodies recovered from the rubble every day.
Lead poisoning of children
The health consequences of Israel's blockade are becoming increasingly apparent, with shortages of basic supplies creating life-threatening risks.
On Monday, the Palestinian health ministry reported that a child had died from severe lead poisoning after being exposed to battery repairs carried out by his father in displacement camps and tents.
Hospital officials told the Palestinian news agency Wafa that the child's death was linked to Israel's ongoing ban on new batteries entering Gaza.
The ban has forced Palestinians to repair damaged and worn-out batteries in cramped, poorly ventilated living spaces.
Health officials believe thousands of other children could be suffering from undiagnosed chronic lead poisoning because Israel also bans the laboratory tests and equipment needed to detect it.
Elsewhere in Gaza, Israeli forces continued demolishing and bombing Palestinian homes, while gunfire and artillery shelling targeted several areas, particularly Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.
There have also been reports of casualties, but health authorities have not yet released figures.

items.title: Israeli MP invokes internment of Japanese Americans in call to restrict Palestinian citizens
items.content:
Israeli MP invokes internment of Japanese Americans in call to restrict Palestinian citizens
Submitted by
Nadav Rapaport
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 11:37
Likud lawmaker Eli Goldschmidt draws parallels with the mass incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II, prompting accusations of unrestrained incitement against Palestinians in Israel
Demonstrators gathered in the Carmel Center for a protest calling for the formation of a new Israeli government that includes Arab political parties (Jess Flom/JNA Press/Sipa USA via Reuters)
Off
An
Israeli
MP from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has invoked the mass incarceration of people of Japanese descent in the United States during World War II while discussing how Palestinian citizens of Israel should be treated.
“When the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbour, President Roosevelt signed an order to place all citizens of Japanese descent in internment camps. How is that different from our situation?” newly elected Knesset member Eli Goldschmidt
told Channel 14 News
on Sunday.
“We are still at war. We have not yet finished dealing with Hamas; we have Arab terrorism in Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] and problems in southern Lebanon,” Goldschmidt added.
“We cannot allow people who are relatives of those who want to destroy us to be privy to confidential information,” the Likud MP said, referring to Palestinian lawmakers from Ra’am and the Joint List.
Goldschmidt was referring to the controversial executive order signed by US President Franklin D Roosevelt in 1942, which forced the relocation and incarceration of more than 100,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them US citizens.
Palestinian citizens of Israel
are descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the 1948 Nakba, during which Zionist militias expelled around 750,000 Palestinians to establish the State of Israel.
Despite being granted Israeli citizenship, they have long faced discrimination and incitement.
They number around two million, accounting for approximately 20 percent of Israel’s population.
Since the Palestinian-led Ra’am and Joint List parties won a historic 19 seats in the Knesset in last month’s elections, Netanyahu and his allies have led a campaign of incitement against Palestinians in Israel, portraying the two parties as “terrorism supporters” in an effort to prevent the formation of a government reliant on their backing.
Violence against Palestinians inside Israel has since increased. Last week, a mosque in the village of Ed-Dahi, near Afula, was set on fire in a suspected
arson attack
linked to an Israeli mob.
'Unrestrained incitement'
Later in the interview, Goldschmidt appeared to distance himself from Roosevelt’s executive order, while maintaining that “a democracy at war should prioritise the security consideration”.
“Roosevelt went too far, but the principle of standing firm on security priorities is right for a country in a state of war,” he
said
.
'It is difficult to comprehend just how far the incitement in Likud has gone, and how it continues to escalate without any restraint'
- Yousef Jabareen, Joint List leader
“I am not recommending that we do what Roosevelt did, but I do suggest not relying on Arab parties in forming a government during wartime.”
Since anti-Netanyahu parties won 67 Knesset seats in the elections, opposition parties, including those led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, have been scrambling to form a new government. However, right-wing parties within the bloc have refused to rely on Ra’am and the Joint List.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List,
condemned
Goldschmidt’s remarks, writing in a post on X: “It is difficult to comprehend just how far the incitement in Likud has gone, and how it continues to escalate without any restraint.”
Jabareen said Goldschmidt was “effectively calling for placing all Arab citizens in the country in internment camps”, describing the remarks as “shocking statements”.
“We must not remain silent in the face of this incitement, and above all, they must not remain in power for even one more day. They are an existential threat to all of us,” the Palestinian leader said, referring to the Likud-led government.

items.title: Israeli strike kills Unrwa worker in Gaza, the UN Palestinian agency says
items.content:
Israeli strike kills Unrwa worker in Gaza, the UN Palestinian agency says
An Israeli air strike killed a man working for the UN Palestinian refugee agency Unrwa in the Gaza Strip on Monday, the relief agency and local health officials said.
The Palestinian man, whom medics named as Adel al-Helo, was working near a water well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the enclave's north, Unrwa and medics said. Three others were wounded in the strike, they said.
"The initial reports indicate that the strike hit a target on the street near the water well, which was manned by Unrwa staff and a guard. The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations," an Unrwa spokesperson told Reuters.
Reporting by Reuters

items.title: Ukraine claims drone attack that sank Russian warship at Libyan naval base
items.content:
Ukraine claims drone attack that sank Russian warship at Libyan naval base
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/23/2026 - 10:30
Zelensky said seven Ukrainian sea drones struck the corvette at the Benghazi naval base, while the UN called for an independent investigation
Satellite image shows a capsized Russian ship at Benghazi port after a suspected drone strike in eastern Libya, 22 November 2026 (Vantor/AFP)
Off
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a
Russian
warship at a naval base in eastern
Libya
, in a major expansion of its maritime campaign against Moscow that has brought the nearly five-year war into the Mediterranean.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones to attack the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday.
The attack, which took place about 2,400km from Ukraine's front line, was among Kyiv's most far-reaching operations against Russian naval assets since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
“Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” Zelensky said in a post on X on Monday.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” he added.
Ukraine's internal security agency, known as the SBU, described the operation as “unique”, saying the Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which it accused Moscow of using to transport military equipment.
The SBU said the naval drones were launched from a “mothership” near the target and that Russian forces attempted to intercept them using air, sea and land defences.
Why Russia remains stubbornly insignificant to the Middle East
Read More »
“Ukraine's defence forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea,” the agency said.
Two Libyan military officials said that the strike severely damaged the corvette and triggered a fire at the naval base, AP reported.
They said at least four drones had been intercepted, while two struck the vessel.
Satellite imagery released by Vantor showed the ship capsized at the port after the explosion.
The Guardian also reported that satellite images indicated the vessel had sunk.
A Libyan official said that at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded.
The country's eastern-based authorities said emergency crews extinguished the fire.
Call for investigation
The strike has raised concerns about the growing involvement of Libya in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, particularly amid reports that Ukrainian military personnel and drone specialists have been operating in the country's western regions.
The eastern-based Libyan government said the Merkury had docked at Benghazi to refuel and take on supplies while returning to Russia under a cooperation agreement with the administration.
Russia ties Black Sea grain deal with Ukraine to halt in oil refinery strikes
Read More »
Osama Hammad, head of the eastern-based government, said he had requested an international investigation through the UN General Assembly and Security Council.
The United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks at Benghazi port and off the city's coast, calling for an immediate investigation.
“Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” the mission said in a statement on Sunday.
It called for an “immediate, independent and transparent investigation” to establish what happened and hold those responsible to account.
Libya has been divided between rival administrations for over a decade, following the 2011 uprising that toppled longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
The internationally recognised Government of National Unity, led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, is based in Tripoli and controls much of the west.
A rival administration operates in the east, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army, which has maintained ties with Russia.

items.title: Israeli army demolishes one of the last Palestinian communities in Jordan Valley
items.content:
Israeli army demolishes one of the last Palestinian communities in Jordan Valley
The Israeli army has destroyed one of the last Palestinian communities in the Jordan Valley in the occupied West Bank.
Khirbet Samra, a Palestinian Bedouin herding community, had all structures and infrastructure demolished in an army operation on Sunday.
Alon Cohen of Bimkom – Planners for Planning Rights told Haaretz that the demolition had been "cruel and illegal."
"Most of the structures and the electricity and water systems had no demolition orders at all. Furthermore, there were five orders issued about 17 years ago, and no structure could be demolished based on them," he said.

items.title: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
items.content:
Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped
The
Trump administration
recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.
Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

items.title: EU sanctions package intended to ‘keep pressure’ on Russia and ‘strike harder’ at its ability to fund Ukraine war – as it happened
items.content:
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen sets out 22nd package of sanctions
Turning to Ukraine, Nato’s Rutte stresses the need to secure the flow of “crucial supplies” or air defence weapons and ammunition to Ukraine.
“
It helps Ukraine to defend itself today, but it also strengthens Ukraine’s hands in any future negotiations with Russia. … But support needs to be concrete.
We have to show Putin that his attempts to weaken our support will fail.”
“Our citizens need to know that the lights will stay on, that their homes will stay warm, that hospitals, transport and communications will keep working.”
“One day it can be in the form of an arson attack against a factory or drones disrupt disrupting an airport. The next, it is sabotaged railways or cargo vessels targeted at sea and cyber-attacks.”
“It’s all happening now, and it won’t go away anytime soon. …
The conclusion of all of this is that we are all targeted,
that we are all affected – when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids and our economies – and they are all interconnected. … That means that we are all in this for the long term, and
therefore we must step up to the plate, to ensure that, we stay ahead of danger.”
“But if we are serious about keeping our alliance strong and secure, then
all allies must pull their weight not only in 2035, but starting now.
At least, everybody needs to have the credible path to get there.”
“These investments are also a boon to prosperity. There are dividends to be gained from investing more in defence. This is about real jobs for real people.”

items.content:

The blockade on Iran-related oil exports was imposed on April 13, lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran, then restored on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.
(Reporting by Elwely Elwelly; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

items.content:

Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, claimed on Monday that critics of the
“accelerating capability and protecting bases” bill
were “jump[ing] at shadows”, accusing them of “absurd” claims. But parliamentary crossbenchers opposed to the bill, which was rushed through parliament with little public scrutiny, were joined on Monday by Prof Anne Twomey, who expressed alarm about what she called an increasing trend of ministers exercising discretionary powers without parliamentary oversight.

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said that Tehran can "act very quickly" to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, granted that the US complies with the country's demands. "Iran remains steadfast in honouring its commitments and will fulfil them as soon as possible, provided the other side complies with the relevant conditions," Baqaei said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is urging Trump to carry out strikes on Iran "as soon as possible", according to Israel’s public broadcaster Kan. The report, published on Sunday, indicated that Trump has yet to make a decision on the matter is reluctant to do so.
US president Donald Trump claimed that he predicted a stock market decline as well as harsher attacks from Iran after the Democratic victory in the recent midterm elections. Trump went onto describe the elections as "very strange". He also questioned the drop in oil prices, saying: "Isn’t it interesting that Oil prices have dropped precipitously after the Midterm Elections? I said that was going to happen. The whole thing is a Giant Hoax!"
A Saudi attack on Yemen's key port city of Hodeida killed at least four people and injured 18 others, according to Houthi-affiliated media. The strike reportedly targeted a building belonging to Yemen's Public Telecommunications Corporation.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said that a motion to extend the deployment of the Cheonghae anti-piracy unit in the Gulf of Aden did not amount to involvement in the US-Israeli war on Iran. Instead, he cited a rise in piracy alongside efforts to protect South Korean ships and citizens using the maritime route.

items.title: Iran says it can reopen Hormuz Strait if US meets conditions
items.content:
Iran says it can reopen Hormuz Strait if US meets conditions
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said that Tehran can "act very quickly" to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, granted that the US complies with the country's demands.
"Iran remains steadfast in honouring its commitments and will fulfil them as soon as possible, provided the other side complies with the relevant conditions," Baqaei said.
He added that Tehran "knows its objectives and the rights of the Iranian people" and that "it will not retreat from defending these rights".

items.title: From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
items.content:
From arson to land seizures: Settlers tighten grip on Palestinian villages near Ramallah
In a series of coordinated attacks across several villages near the city of Ramallah in the central occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers torched Palestinian vehicles between Saturday evening and Sunday morning.
The settlers also spray-painted racist slogans on the walls of homes in the three villages, calling for the killing of Arabs and for revenge against them.
Rafat Abu Musa, head of the village council of Deir al-Sudan, north of Ramallah, told Middle East Eye that settlers infiltrated the southern part of the village at 11.30pm on Saturday and burned down two vehicles.
They spray-painted slogans in Hebrew on the walls of nearby houses, he said, adding that the same area had been targeted by a similar attack two months ago, during which a vehicle was set on fire.
Abu Musa indicated that the settlers came from a newly built outpost on the summit of Jabal al-Ras, located in the neighbouring village of Umm Safa.

items.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
items.content:
In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions
Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.
That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

items.title: Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
items.content:
Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, says that the destruction unfolding in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon is part of a longer history of anti-Muslim racism that has made mass Muslim suffering and death politically permissible.
She says that Islamophobia is not simply a matter of prejudice or discrimination, but a global system of racial power that constructs Muslims and those identified as Muslim as security threats, allowing violence against them to be justified in the name of security.
Central to this system is the figure of the Muslim terrorist, which portrays Muslim political agency as inherently threatening. Shareef says that this logic extends beyond surveillance, detention and militarised borders to warfare, political abandonment and the destruction of the conditions necessary for life.
She identifies Palestine as a key site where contemporary security practices and technologies of control have been refined and reproduced elsewhere, a process she describes through the concept of the “Palestine boomerang”. Although conflicts in Iran, Lebanon, Kashmir, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan have distinct histories, she argues that they reveal a recurring pattern in which Muslim populations are portrayed as threats and their suffering becomes easier to justify.
Shareef concludes that confronting anti-Muslim racism is ultimately a struggle to protect life and human dignity. She calls for sustained resistance to systems that expose entire populations to premature death, arguing that the responsibility to seek justice remains even when the outcome is uncertain.

items.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
items.content:
Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group
Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.
Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.
